summary:
We developed EarthEcho – Hear How Places Change, an interactive web platform that transforms NASA Earth-observation data into sound through data sonification. 

Our platform includes three features: Earth at Night, which converts satellite images of nighttime lights (2012–2023) into musical notes based on brightness; a Temperature Map, which translates temperature variations into different pitches; and an image upload feature that allows users to explore image brightness through sound.

EarthEcho addresses the challenge by providing an alternative way to interpret complex scientific datasets, making environmental information more interactive, engaging, and accessible. By translating visual data into audio, it also enables visually impaired individuals to experience geographical and environmental patterns.

This project is important because access to scientific knowledge should not depend solely on visual abilities. EarthEcho encourages environmental awareness, promotes inclusive science education, and makes NASA’s valuable Earth-observation data accessible to a wider audience.
details:
EarthEcho is a website that lets you explore Earth through sound. It takes NASA imagery and temperature data and turns them into something you can hear, alongside the usual maps, dates and numbers. We built it for The Earth Information Jukebox challenge, mainly with blind and low-vision learners, teachers and mixed-ability classrooms in mind. It’s free, public and you don’t need an account.

The night-light part covers South Asia, Europe and the eastern United States for every year from 2012 to 2023. That’s 36 regional views, all built from NASA Scientific Visualization Studio imagery. In guided mode the app sweeps west to east across 32 vertical strips. Each strip plays a pitch based on how bright it is, and the strip lights up on screen so you can see what you’re hearing. In free exploration you drag a small sampling patch around the image, resize it and hear the result right away. You can also move around with the keyboard.

Comparing things is really the heart of it. You can play the same strip in 2012 and then in 2023, or listen to it change across all 12 years. We kept the mappings fixed across dates, so differences aren’t exaggerated by rescaling each image separately. For example, South Asia’s ninth strip comes out at about 293.7 Hz in 2012 and 440.0 Hz in 2023. These tones come from NASA’s rendered night-light images. They aren’t direct measurements of population, electricity use or economic activity.

There’s also a Temperature map tab. It uses NASA POWER monthly mean air temperature at two metres for every month of 2024, which works out to 137,844 cell/month values across the three regions. You can click on cells, hear a whole row, or follow a single cell from January to December. Colour and pitch use the same fixed −20°C to 50°C range, and the actual temperature number is always there too. If a value is missing it stays silent instead of pretending to be 0°C. For the grid cell near Peshawar (34.00°N, 71.875°E), it’s 11.03°C in January and 33.34°C in July. That shows the seasons changing within 2024. It doesn’t show a long-term climate trend.

Beyond Earth, the image collection includes Andromeda, the Carina Nebula, a Hubble star cluster and EPIC Earth imagery. You can also open your own image, which stays local in your browser, or pull the latest published NASA EPIC photo. That photo is clearly dated, so it’s not passed off as a live feed. You can export WAV audio, processing notes and temperature CSVs, and there’s an option to save the whole app and its assets for offline use.

It’s built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript modules, Canvas and the Web Audio API. We used Python, NumPy, Pillow and ImageMagick to prepare the data and Node.js for the build and tests, and the site is hosted on Vercel. The core experience doesn’t need a paid API key, an account, a database or any AI service. All the sound is generated in the browser, and it comes out the same every time. Our processing records source hashes and crop boundaries, keeps 16-bit source precision for the guided night-light features, and leaves the temperature grid as is, with no interpolation.

What we think is new about EarthEcho is how it puts together controlled comparisons, free exploration and data-to-sound choices you can trace back, all in an atlas that’s actually usable. Along with the visual design, we thought about scientific accuracy, keyboard access, predictable audio controls, privacy, bandwidth and reproducibility. It could be used for classroom investigations, community STEM workshops, exploring at home, or teachers making their own sound clips. One deployment we’d like to pursue is a listening station at a science centre. Next, we’d start by testing with blind and low-vision users, then add guided lessons and translated instructions, and only after that add more regions or new well-documented data layers. Touch and haptic features are ideas we’re exploring for later. To be clear, these are plans. We haven’t deployed EarthEcho at any institution or measured learning outcomes yet.

The repository has 89 automated checks, plus extra browser, export and responsive-layout checks. That shows the app works technically. We still need to test it with blind and low-vision users before we can say it improves learning or is properly accessible.

We used OpenAI Codex only for data cleaning, testing and submission preparation. We did the design, the data-to-sound mapping and the main development ourselves. None of the NASA imagery is AI-generated. We looked at the Earths-Jukebox repository for ideas while reviewing our architecture, but we didn’t copy any of its code.
